title: “I AM THAT I AM” — or “I am the one who is”?
summary: In the KJV, with the Hebrew, God answers Moses with a first-person verb repeated: “I Am That I Am”, and “I Am hath sent me”. Brenton’s Greek has a different construction: “I am the one who is”, and “the one who is has sent me”.

title: Did Amram marry his father’s sister, or his father’s brother’s daughter?

title: “Moses feared” and fled from Pharaoh — or left Egypt “not fearing the wrath of the king”?
summary: Exodus says Moses feared when his killing of the Egyptian became known, and fled from the face of Pharaoh, who sought to slay him. Hebrews says that by faith he forsook Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king.
text: KJV Exodus 2:14: “And Moses feared, and said, Surely this thing is known.” KJV 2:15: “Now when Pharaoh heard this thing, he sought to slay Moses. But Moses fled from the face of Pharaoh, and dwelt in the land of Midian”. Hebrew (WLC) 2:14: וַיִּירָ֤א מֹשֶׁה֙ [and Moses feared]. 2:15: וַיִּבְרַ֤ח מֹשֶׁה֙ מִפְּנֵ֣י פַרְעֹ֔ה [and Moses fled from the face of Pharaoh]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2:14: ἐφοβήθη δὲ Μωυσῆς [and Moses feared]. 2:15: Ἀνεχώρησε δὲ Μωυσῆς ἀπὸ προσώπου Φαραὼ [and Moses withdrew from the face of Pharaoh]. KJV Hebrews 11:27: “By faith he forsook Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king”. Greek New Testament (TISCH; TR has the same words) Hebrews 11:27: πίστει κατέλιπεν Αἴγυπτον, μὴ φοβηθεὶς τὸν θυμὸν τοῦ βασιλέως [by faith he left Egypt, not fearing the anger of the king]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/2/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO02.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/TISCH/58/11/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/TR/58/11/.
reasoning: Exodus tells of one occasion on which Moses left Egypt with a king angry at him: Pharaoh sought to slay him and he fled. Of that occasion it says in so many words that Moses feared. Hebrews says he forsook Egypt not fearing the wrath of the king. The verb for fearing in the Greek of Exodus 2:14 and in Hebrews 11:27 is the same.
scope: No tag is proposed: the Hebrew and Brenton’s Greek agree with the KJV in Exodus. The two statements clash if Hebrews 11:27 refers to the flight to Midian. They can be reconciled if Hebrews refers instead to the later departure with all Israel, or if the fear in Exodus 2:14 is fear of discovery and not of the king’s wrath; Hebrews does not say which departure it means, and it mentions the passover only in the next verse. This record does not decide between those readings. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. title: No steps to the altar — yet Ezekiel’s altar has stairs
summary: In Exodus the Lord forbids going up by steps to his altar. In Ezekiel the altar whose measures and ordinances are given in the Lord’s name has stairs that face east.
text: KJV Exodus 20:26: “Neither shalt thou go up by steps unto mine altar, that thy nakedness be not discovered thereon.” Hebrew (WLC) 20:26: וְלֹֽא־תַעֲלֶ֥ה בְמַעֲלֹ֖ת עַֽל־מִזְבְּחִ֑י [and you shall not go up by steps upon my altar]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 20:26: Οὐκ ἀναβήσῃ ἐν ἀναβαθμίσιν ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιαστήριόν μου [you shall not go up by steps upon my altar]. KJV Ezekiel 43:17: “and his stairs shall look toward the east”. KJV 43:18: “thus saith the Lord God; These are the ordinances of the altar in the day when they shall make it, to offer burnt offerings thereon”. Hebrew (WLC) Ezekiel 43:17: וּמַעֲלֹתֵ֖הוּ פְּנֹ֥ות קָדִֽים [and its steps face east]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 43:17: καὶ οἱ κλημακτῆρες αὐτοῦ βλέποντες κατὰ ἀνατολάς [and its steps looking toward the east]. KJV Exodus 28:42: “And thou shalt make them linen breeches to cover their nakedness”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/20/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/26/43/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO20.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EZK43.htm.
reasoning: Exodus 20:26 forbids steps up to the Lord’s altar. Ezekiel 43:17 gives the altar stairs, and the next verse presents the altar’s ordinances as the word of the Lord. The Hebrew uses the same noun for the forbidden steps and for the stairs of Ezekiel’s altar. Since the stairs are part of what is commanded, this is a contrast between two commands, not a breach of law by anyone.
scope: No tag is proposed: the Hebrew and Brenton’s Greek agree with the KJV in both verses. The two can be reconciled in more than one way. The rule in Exodus follows a law about altars of earth and unhewn stone and may be limited to those; its stated reason, nakedness, is met for the priests by the linen breeches of Exodus 28:42; and Ezekiel’s altar is seen in a vision of a house not yet built. Neither passage states any of these as the reason the rule does not apply. The steps of altars in other books were not examined. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. title: Silver from 603,550 men numbered — a month before the numbering that gives that total
summary: The silver for the sockets of the tabernacle came from 603,550 men who were numbered, and the tabernacle was reared on the first day of the first month of the second year. The numbering that yields 603,550 is commanded on the first day of the second month of that year.
text: KJV Exodus 38:25: “And the silver of them that were numbered of the congregation was an hundred talents”. KJV 38:26: “for every one that went to be numbered, from twenty years old and upward, for six hundred thousand and three thousand and five hundred and fifty men”. KJV 38:27: “And of the hundred talents of silver were cast the sockets of the sanctuary”. KJV Exodus 40:17: “And it came to pass in the first month in the second year, on the first day of the month, that the tabernacle was reared up.” KJV Numbers 1:1: “on the first day of the second month, in the second year after they were come out of the land of Egypt”. KJV 1:46: “Even all they that were numbered were six hundred thousand and three thousand and five hundred and fifty.” Hebrew (WLC) Exodus 38:26: לְשֵׁשׁ־מֵאֹ֥ות אֶ֙לֶף֙ וּשְׁלֹ֣שֶׁת אֲלָפִ֔ים וַחֲמֵ֥שׁ מֵאֹ֖ות וַחֲמִשִּֽׁים [for six hundred thousand and three thousand and five hundred and fifty]. Numbers 1:1: בְּאֶחָד֩ לַחֹ֨דֶשׁ הַשֵּׁנִ֜י בַּשָּׁנָ֣ה הַשֵּׁנִ֗ית [on the first of the second month, in the second year]. Numbers 1:46: שֵׁשׁ־מֵאֹ֥ות אֶ֖לֶף וּשְׁלֹ֣שֶׁת אֲלָפִ֑ים וַחֲמֵ֥שׁ מֵאֹ֖ות וַחֲמִשִּֽׁים [six hundred thousand and three thousand and five hundred and fifty]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek), where the passage is printed as Exodus 39:3: εἰς τὰς ἑξήκοντα μυριάδας, καὶ τρισχίλιοι πεντακόσιοι καὶ πεντήκοντα [for the sixty ten-thousands, and three thousand five hundred and fifty]. Numbers 1:46: ἑξακόσιαι χιλιάδες καὶ τρισχίλιοι καὶ πεντακόσιοι καὶ πεντήκοντα [six hundred thousand and three thousand and five hundred and fifty]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/38/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/4/1/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO39.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/NUM01.htm.
reasoning: The sockets were cast from the silver of those numbered, so that numbering was complete before the tabernacle was reared on the first day of the first month. The numbering in Numbers is commanded a month later, on the first day of the second month, and its total is the same figure to the last man: 603,550. Either one numbering is placed at two different times, or two numberings a month or more apart gave an identical total.
scope: No tag is proposed: the Hebrew and Brenton’s Greek have the same total as the KJV in both books. In Brenton’s Greek the chapters on the making of the tabernacle are in a different order, and KJV 38:26 is printed as 39:3. The two accounts can be reconciled if there were two numberings with the same result, or if the half-shekel of Exodus was gathered earlier and its count reused in Numbers; neither book says so. The count in Numbers leaves out the Levites (Numbers 1:47), and Exodus 38 does not say whether its count does. No claim is made about the actual number of the people. title: The “Red sea” — the Hebrew says “sea of suph”, and has no word for red
summary: Where the KJV has “the Red sea”, the Hebrew has “sea of suph”. The KJV renders the same word suph as “flags” at Exodus 2:3 and “weeds” at Jonah 2:5. The Hebrew has no word for “red” in these verses. Brenton’s Greek has “Red sea”, as the KJV does.
text: KJV Exodus 10:19: “cast them into the Red sea”. KJV 13:18: “through the way of the wilderness of the Red sea”. KJV 15:4: “his chosen captains also are drowned in the Red sea”. KJV 15:22: “So Moses brought Israel from the Red sea”. Hebrew (WLC) 10:19: וַיִּתְקָעֵ֖הוּ יָ֣מָּה סּ֑וּף [and drove it to the sea of suph]. 13:18: דֶּ֥רֶךְ הַמִּדְבָּ֖ר יַם־ס֑וּף [by the way of the wilderness, the sea of suph]. 15:4: טֻבְּע֥וּ בְיַם־סֽוּף [were sunk in the sea of suph]. 15:22: מִיַּם־ס֔וּף [from the sea of suph]. KJV Exodus 2:3: “and she laid it in the flags by the river”. Hebrew (WLC) 2:3: וַתָּ֥שֶׂם בַּסּ֖וּף עַל־שְׂפַ֥ת הַיְאֹֽר [and she put it in the suph on the bank of the river]. KJV Jonah 2:5: “the weeds were wrapped about my head”. Hebrew (WLC) 2:6 (KJV 2:5): ס֖וּף חָב֥וּשׁ לְרֹאשִֽׁי [suph was bound to my head]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 10:19: εἰς τὴν ἐρυθρὰν θαλάσσαν [into the Red sea]. 13:18: εἰς τὴν ἐρυθρὰν θάλασσαν [to the Red sea]. 15:4: κατεπόθησαν ἐν ἐρυθρᾷ θαλάσσῃ [were swallowed up in the Red sea]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/10/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/13/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/15/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/2/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/32/2/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO10.htm, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO13.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO15.htm.
reasoning: The Hebrew name of the sea is made of two words: “sea” and suph. Suph is a word for water plants: the KJV itself has “flags” for it where the infant Moses is laid by the river, and “weeds” where Jonah speaks of the deep. So the Hebrew name says “sea of reeds” or “sea of weeds”. “Red” is a different meaning, and no Hebrew word for red stands in any of these verses. The KJV’s “Red sea” matches the Greek name, not the Hebrew one.
scope: H applies at Exodus 10:19, 13:18, 15:4 and 15:22, the four verses of Exodus quoted; the name occurs in other verses of the KJV that were not individually compared. Brenton’s Greek agrees with the KJV here, so no G is proposed. The finding is about what the name says, not about where the sea is: “Red sea” may be the customary name of the same water, and this record does not claim that the KJV points to the wrong sea or that the sea crossed was a marsh or a lake.
